Friday, 10 pm
Third time this month. Gopika stopped at my desk at 4:45 and said, "Nandini, your slides are always so elegant, I don't know how you do it." Two minutes later: "Could you take over the vendor report? Just this once?"
On Monday it was "you're the only one here who really gets spreadsheets" before asking me to fix her sheet. Last week, "you're such a good listener", then could I cover her Saturday.
Tonight I scrolled back through my messages. Every compliment from her came within ten minutes of a favour. When my manager praises me, she names something specific, like the chart on page six, and she does it when she wants nothing.
Maybe Gopika is overloaded and doesn't know how to ask. Maybe it's habit. Either way, next time I'll thank her for the kind words and decide about the favour separately.

At the government school in the small town, Sharmila had started keeping a mental diary about her colleague Akash.
On Monday, he said her lesson plans were "a work of art." On Tuesday, he asked her to take his exam duty on Saturday.
Two weeks later, he told her she was "the only teacher here who really cares." That afternoon he asked if she could check his thirty science notebooks, "just this once."
Today, in the staffroom, he praised her new sari in front of everyone. Sharmila smiled politely and waited.
Sure enough, at lunch: "Sharmila ji, the district meeting on Friday, could you go instead of me?"
She put down her tiffin. She didn't feel angry, exactly, more tired. Real praise from the headmistress was always about something specific she'd done. Akash's always came just before a favour.
"I can't this Friday," she said. "But your meeting notes from last month were very clear. You'll do well."

qa.a: He asked if she could go to the district meeting on Friday instead of him.

qa.a: Sharmila felt tired and wary rather than angry, recognising that Akash's praise always came just before a favour.

qa.a: She said no to the request, kept it polite, and gave him one specific, sincere compliment of her own that didn't depend on a yes.

In the Lisbon software office, Pablo sat two desks from Paulo, and by March he had noticed something.
"Your code is genius, man," Paulo said on Monday, leaning over Pablo's screen. "Honestly, you're the best developer on this floor." Pablo smiled. It felt good.
On Monday afternoon: "Hey, could you cover my weekend on-call?"
Two weeks later: "You're the only person here with real taste." Ten minutes later: "Could you review my pull request tonight? It's urgent."
Pablo started to notice the rhythm. The compliments were big and vague. They never mentioned anything specific he had actually done. And they always arrived just before a request.
His team lead, by contrast, had once written: "Your fix to the payment retry saved us a whole weekend." Nothing more. No request.
The next time Paulo called him a genius, Pablo just said, "Thanks. What do you need?" Paulo laughed awkwardly and told him.

qa.q: What had Pablo's team lead written?
qa.a: "Your fix to the payment retry saved us a whole weekend."

qa.q: How did Pablo feel once he noticed the rhythm?
qa.a: Pablo felt wary and a little let down, realising the flattering words were steering him toward favours.

qa.q: What did Pablo do that helped him not be steered?
qa.a: He thanked Paulo and asked directly what he needed, separating the compliment from the request.

qa.q: How did Paulo seem to feel when Pablo asked what he needed?
qa.a: Paulo seemed awkward and caught out, laughing uneasily before admitting the request.

grounding: It shows a colleague noticing that vague compliments always arrive right before a request, unlike sincere, specific praise.

The NGO office was tiny, so Parul heard everything Minakshi said to the new programme manager.
"Your presentation was so inspiring, Sir. Honestly, this office needed a leader like you."
Parul watched Minakshi linger at his door, then add, "Sir, about the Delhi conference, I'd be the perfect person to go."
It was the third time this month. The week before, it had been "You have such vision" before asking for Friday off. Before that, "You're so approachable" before asking to skip the field visit.
Parul felt a small, uncomfortable knot. She liked Minakshi. But the praise was always big, never about anything particular, and always followed by an ask.
When the manager later praised Parul, he said, "Your field report from Barmer was the clearest I've read." Specific. Nothing wanted. Parul realised she trusted that kind of praise more, and she decided to stop taking Minakshi's words at face value.

qa.a: She asked to be the person who goes to the Delhi conference.

qa.a: Parul felt a small, uncomfortable knot, liking Minakshi but noticing the praise always led to a request.

qa.q: What difference did Parul notice between the two kinds of praise?
qa.a: Minakshi's praise was big and vague and came before a request, while the manager's praise was specific and wanted nothing.

qa.a: The manager might feel less flattered and more cautious, realising the compliments were aimed at getting favours.
